data.title: Japan tobacco faces record loss after losing Russian units
data.description:
Japan Tobacco expects to post a record consolidated net loss of JPY724bn (about $4.6bn) for the year to December, Jiji Press reported on November 21. The loss follows the company's removal of its Russian subsidiaries from its consolidated accounts after it lost practical control of them.

The forecast has raised concern in Tokyo because the Japanese government is JT's biggest shareholder, with roughly a third of its outstanding shares. The state uses the dividends it receives from the tobacco group to help pay for industrial investment under the fiscal investment and loan programme, so a weaker JT could hit that funding stream.

Russia has been one of JT's most important markets. The company entered the country in 1999, and the business there has generated around 25% of the group's adjusted operating profit.

JT kept its Russian business running after Moscow began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, even as other foreign companies pulled out. Its position changed this month, when Russian President Vladimir Putin signed an executive order handing seven JT subsidiaries over to local management.

That decree left the Japanese company without meaningful authority over the units, forcing it to deconsolidate them and book the charge behind the expected annual loss.

The size of the projected loss is the largest in JT's history. Jiji Press described the worsening results as a serious setback for the government, given its reliance on the company's payouts.

data.title: Japan listed firms' profits surge 47% on AI boom
data.description:
Combined net profit at companies listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange rose 46.9% year on year to JPY28.9346 trillion ($182.4bn) in the six months to September 2026, the first increase in three years, Yomiuri Shimbun reported on November 21. Robust orders linked to artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres lifted earnings across a wide range of industries.

The gain was driven by demand for the semiconductors needed to run AI systems, which pushed profits higher well beyond the chip sector itself. Nearly all companies have now released their interim results for the period.

SMBC Nikko Securities compiled the figures from 988 companies in the Tokopix (TOPIX) index that had reported by November 19, accounting for 99.6% of the index's constituents. The tally excludes financial companies and SoftBank Group.

Manufacturers led the rise, with net profit up 69.2% to JPY18.3497 trillion as chip demand increased. The electrical equipment category, which includes memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings, nearly doubled its profit with a 98.5% rise. Chemicals companies, a group that covers semiconductor materials suppliers, posted a 30.7% increase.

Non-manufacturers reported a smaller gain, with combined net profit climbing 19.7% to JPY10.5849 trillion.

data.description: Australian stocks are poised to keep falling at the start of the week, following U.S. equities deeper into the red. data.title: Strategy hints at more Bitcoin purchases after $33M buy
data.description:
Strategy Inc. added 485 Bitcoin to its balance sheet last week. That brings the company's total stash to 850,849 BTC.

The purchase cost approximately $33.4 million, a modest outlay by Strategy's standards. Executive Chairman Michael Saylor is already hinting that the next one is coming.

According to an SEC Form 8-K filed on November 16, 2026, Strategy bought the 485 BTC between November 9 and November 15. The average price came to $68,887 per coin.

That figure matters because it sits below the company's overall average acquisition price of $75,452 per BTC.

Across its full treasury, the company has spent about $64.20 billion building its position. Its 850,849 BTC represent about 4.05% of Bitcoin's maximum supply of 21 million coins.

The latest buy was smaller than some of Strategy's recent weekly purchases. Prior acquisitions have included a 1,036 BTC tranche, so weekly volumes have swung noticeably.

The funding came entirely from net proceeds of MSTR common stock sales. Strategy issues new shares into the market, collects the cash, and converts it into Bitcoin.

Notably, the Bitcoin buy was not the biggest check Strategy wrote that week. During the same period, the company repurchased $228.1 million of its STRC preferred stock.

That buyback was several times larger than the Bitcoin purchase.

The broader picture is less cheerful than the headline holdings figure. Strategy's Bitcoin treasury has reportedly traded below its cost basis, leaving the company with unrealized losses of around $9.61 billion.

Market action has not helped. On November 22, Bitcoin dipped to around $55,000 before recovering above $60,000.

Both levels sit well under Strategy's $75,452 average cost.

That same day, Saylor posted a short message on social media.

"The dots aren't done."

The remark fits his long-running habit of teasing purchases before the official disclosures land.

None of this confirms a new acquisition. Until Strategy files paperwork with the SEC, the post remains a hint rather than a transaction.

Strategy, formerly known as MicroStrategy, has spent years transforming itself into a corporate Bitcoin treasury. The rebrand reflected what investors already understood: the company's identity is now tied to its BTC holdings.

Its playbook has been consistent. Raise capital through equity and other instruments, then route the proceeds into Bitcoin, often on a weekly cadence.

The first takeaway is that Strategy's commitment does not appear to depend on being in the green. The company kept buying at $68,887 per coin while sitting on billions in paper losses.

The scale of recent purchases is worth watching. A 485 BTC week is a fraction of the 1,036 BTC tranche seen earlier, and the $228.1 million preferred buyback dwarfed the Bitcoin spend.

The next data points to watch are straightforward. Look for whether Saylor's "dots" turn into another 8-K, how large the next purchase is, and how it gets funded.

Watch, too, where Bitcoin trades relative to the $75,452 average cost.

data.title: Corporate America hunts for 'generational' growth in AI, trading cards and the L.A. airport
data.description:
By Bill Peters

There's been no shortage of trends deemed once-in-a-generation by executives on earnings calls

Delta recently praised "generational airport investments" in Los Angeles.

On earnings calls over recent weeks, there's been very little that executives couldn't spin into a "generational" opportunity.

The adjective has come up on numerous calls. Executives have naturally cast artificial intelligence as a "generational" shift. But they've also described a boom in trading cards and flights to Fort Lauderdale, Fla., as "generational." Renovations at Los Angeles International Airport? Also, apparently, "generational."

For instance, Morgan Stanley (MS), during its earnings call last month, said the bank was helping clients stay on top of AI, be it through innovation or matters related to spending on the technology.

"We all see that the power of AI as an efficiency and productivity and resiliency tool is [an] incontrovertible, generational jump in technology," CEO Ted Pick said.

Elsewhere, the investment firm Blackstone (BX) said it had become a crucial provider of capital in the AI landscape, adding that its data-center portfolio rested on solid, long-term contracts with "highly creditworthy counterparties."

"As the AI revolution progresses, the rising demand for capital is creating generational opportunities for those with the platform, relationships, capabilities and discipline to meet this demand," CEO Stephen Schwarzman said on the company's earnings call last month.

Blackrock (BLK), another investment firm, said on its call last month that companies "need to fund a generational AI buildout," and that the firm was at the center of many conversations related to that buildout. And fintech company Fiserv (FISV) said this month that AI had spurred "a generational transformation" in software development.

That generational talk has run up against deeper pressures on the AI trade - which has lately been dogged by concerns over Big Tech's epic spending and borrowing plans to develop the technology, the ouster of Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang and the reality of a Democrat-controlled Congress next year. More broadly, consumers are still navigating higher prices.

Big Tech, and in turn artificial intelligence, have done much of the work to prop up the S&P 500 index SPX over the past few years. However, according to a FactSet report released Friday, the so-called Magnificent Seven tech companies - Apple (AAPL), Amazon.com (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG), Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META), Nvidia and Tesla (TSLA) - reported lower earnings growth than the rest of the index for the third quarter. The S&P 500 is down around 10% over the past month.

Still, "generational" shifts are happening elsewhere. For Hasbro (HAS), which owns the fantasy card game Magic: The Gathering, that shift was happening in trading cards. Sales of the game have hit record levels, as Hasbro leans on rarities and a collectible market for cards that some are increasingly treating like an investment.

"I think trading cards over the last year have emerged as the No. 1 category in toys and games," Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks said in October. "I think they're actually bigger than building blocks now, and we see that as a generational structural shift and not just as kind of, like, a one-time thing."

In October, Boeing (BA) said it had "scored a generational win" with the U.S. Navy, which chose it to build a fighter jet. Kimberly-Clark (KMB) - known for brands like Huggies and Kleenex - described its acquisition of Kenvue this month as a "generational opportunity" to meet consumers' increasingly personalized health and wellness needs.

JetBlue Airways (JBLU) last month described expanded flight service to Fort Lauderdale as a "generational opportunity for us." Even Los Angeles International Airport - long considered a traffic and infrastructure nightmare - got a shout-out from Delta Air Lines (DAL), which has invested money to renovate and connect terminals and expand its lounges at the airport.

Delta's chief commercial officer, Joe Esposito, said on the airline's earnings call last month that it was adding service from Los Angeles to the South Pacific, Hong Kong and Manila, Philippines.

"This has been enabled by generational airport investments at L.A. to create a modern, connected complex with additional gate capacity and seamless access to the international terminal," Esposito said.

-Bill Peters
